extracted.intended_audience: journalists, editors and news publishers (particularly in Australia)
extracted.subtask_description: Standards for news reporting of family and domestic violence court proceedings, especially when individuals seek Family Violence Orders (FVOs), covering privacy, public interest, use of images and steps to avoid harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid intruding on a person's reasonable expectations of privacy (General Principle 5)
rubrics_metrics.description: Publications must take reasonable steps to avoid intruding on a person’s reasonable expectations of privacy, unless doing so is sufficiently in the public interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Council found that even where no suppression order exists, the sensitive nature of proceedings (e.g., an applicant seeking a protection order) can create a reasonable expectation of privacy; naming the applicant and including a prominent photograph was not sufficiently in the public interest to outweigh that expectation. Absence of a suppression order does not automatically remove privacy expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid causing or contributing materially to substantial distress or risk to health or safety (General Principle 6)
rubrics_metrics.description: Publications must take reasonable steps to avoid causing or contributing materially to substantial offence, distress or prejudice, or a substantial risk to health or safety, unless doing so is sufficiently in the public interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identifying a complainant in reports of domestic violence proceedings is likely to cause substantial distress; publishers must have a sufficient public interest justification before publishing material likely to cause such harm. The Council found that naming and showing a prominent photograph was unnecessary and likely to cause substantial distress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open court reporting is permitted but must be fair and balanced
rubrics_metrics.description: Unless otherwise restricted by law or court order, open court hearings are matters of public record and can be reported by the press.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such reports need to be fair and balanced. Reporting that parties and evidence were before the court is in the public interest (for example, that a former minister was subject to proceedings), but that interest does not automatically justify identifying third parties or victims when their identification is not necessary to the reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not identify relatives or friends unless necessary (Privacy Principle 7)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reports should not identify relatives or friends of people accused or convicted of crime unless the reference to them is necessary for the full, fair and accurate reporting of the crime or subsequent legal proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This principle aims to prevent exploitation of members of the public caught up in newsworthy events. In this case the Council noted the complainant was an applicant for a protection order (not merely a relative/friend), so it made no finding under Principle 7, but the principle remains a distinct standard for identification of non‑accused parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Safety and well‑being of those affected by family violence must be primary
rubrics_metrics.description: In reporting on family and domestic violence, the safety and well‑being of those affected must be the primary consideration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advisory Guideline on Family and Domestic Violence Reporting highlights that publications should not publish information that could cause or contribute to risk of harm, offence or distress, and should exercise great care and respect when reporting such matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public interest test must outweigh privacy/harm to justify identification
rubrics_metrics.description: Identification of an individual (name/photo) may only be justified where the public interest in doing so sufficiently outweighs the person's privacy expectations and the risk of harm or distress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is legitimate public interest in reporting the due administration of justice (e.g., that a former minister faced proceedings), but detail such as naming an applicant for an FVO or showing their photograph must be necessary to that public interest. In this case the public interest in reporting the proceedings did not justify naming the complainant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generally avoid naming alleged victims in domestic/family violence reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Media organisations should generally avoid naming alleged victims when reporting on domestic and family violence proceedings held in open court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The publication's own stated policy was to not name alleged victims; exceptions should be rare and require clear public interest justification. Consideration should also be given to the potential deterrent effect on other victims seeking assistance if victims are routinely named.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not publish material (including social media images) that is unnecessary to the report
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishing an individual's name and a prominent photograph was unnecessary and did not add to the report of court proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sourcing a photograph from the person's social media (e.g., Facebook) does not in itself make publication appropriate. Editors must assess whether images materially contribute to accurate, fair reporting or simply increase risk of harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Take reasonable steps to avoid causing substantial distress or risk
rubrics_metrics.description: Publications are required to take reasonable steps to avoid causing substantial distress or creating a substantial risk to health or safety when reporting sensitive matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This includes editorial decisions about naming, imagery, prominence, and whether publication of particular details is necessary. The Council found the publication failed to take such reasonable steps in this case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect a victim's right to refuse or terminate interviews or photographic sessions
rubrics_metrics.description: A victim or bereaved person has the right to refuse or terminate an interview or photographic session at any time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Media organisations should not exploit members of the public caught up in newsworthy events; consent and ongoing willingness to participate must be respected.
